To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
catalepsy is a syndrome of immobility, in which morphine inhibits reflexes used for support and locomotion, while haloperidol inhibits reflexes for orienting, scanning, and walking.
the effects of morphine and haloperidol on the postural support reflex system are not additive but are subtractive and that this subtraction reveals gradients of integration.
the postural support reflex system is organized into subcomponents that can be revealed by subtractive analysis and that the subcomponents are organized in gradients along the body axis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the functional organization of the motor system and with the mechanisms by which it reorganizes itself during recovery.
the mechanisms that control the organization of the motor system, with the mechanisms that regulate motor behavior, and with the mechanisms that underlie the recovery of motor function after damage.
the mechanisms by which the nervous system integrates the subcomponents of postural support reflex systems to produce the coordinated postures and movements of intact animals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

morphine and haloperidol act on different subcomponents of a complex behavior, that these subcomponents are organized along specific body gradients, and that these gradients can be altered by pharmacological agents.
morphine subtracts subreflex components of the postural support reflex to reveal gradients of the integration of their function.
morphine subtracts from haloperidol's postural support reflex effects, and this subtractive action proceeds along gradients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the postural support reflex is a composite of several subcomponents, each of which is integrated at a specific level of the neuraxis.
morphine inhibits the reflexes that are used to maintain stable postures and that, during recovery, the subcomponents are reorganized along gradients of the body axis.
morphine subtracts subcomponent reflexes of haloperidoleffects to reveal gradients of reflex integration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the morphine state is not a unitary phenomenon but is composed of a number of subcomponents, some of which can be isolated and studied independently of others.
morphine reveals the fractional nature of reflexive postural support and that the recovery of these reflexes during the washout of morphine's effect follows a body gradient.
the morphine effect on postural support reflex integration can reveal gradients of integration and that these can be used to study the mechanisms of recovery from catalepsy.
